svg.aria-label: Identifying scrap metal. 1 Magnet: steel, iron and cast iron (and some stainless steels) stick firmly; aluminium, copper, brass, lead, zinc and most stainless steels do not stick. 2 Colour: red is copper, golden yellow is brass (copper and zinc), dull gold or brown is bronze (copper and tin); weight in the hand: very light is aluminium (about 2.7 g/cm³) or the even lighter magnesium (about 1.7 g/cm³); very heavy and soft, marked by a fingernail, is lead (about 11.3 g/cm³). 3 File: if the file will not bite and skids it is hardened steel; if it cuts easily it is mild steel, wrought iron, cast iron or a non-ferrous metal; a clear ring when tapped means steel, a dull sound cast iron or lead; for steel of unknown origin, cut off a small piece, heat it to cherry red and quench in water; if a file will not bite, it is high in carbon and good for cutting tools; if the file bites, it is mild steel. 4 Spark testing (on a grinding wheel or with a coarse file): mild steel (reinforcing bar, iron sheet) gives long straw-yellow streams with very few forks; medium-carbon steel (shafts, gears) fairly long streams with clearly more forks; high-carbon steel (files, springs) shorter streams with many dense forks like clusters of little stars; cast iron short streams, dark red to orange, with a few small forks at the ends; stainless steel fairly short orange-yellow streams with few forks; aluminium, copper, brass and lead almost no sparks; the more the sparks burst, the higher the carbon; compare against a known steel. 5 Metals in a car: the battery is lead with sulphuric acid, not recommended to recycle yourself; the engine block is grey cast iron, pistons and cylinder heads aluminium; brake discs and drums are grey cast iron and cannot be forged; wheel rims are mostly aluminium, some magnesium alloy; the body is mild steel sheet; leaf and coil springs are spring steel (about 0.6% carbon) for knives, axes and chisels; shock absorbers and gas springs contain high-pressure gas and oil, never heat or cut them; leftover petrol vapour in the fuel tank explodes; drive shafts and half-shafts are medium-carbon alloy steel for hammer heads and crowbars. 6 Other sources: files (about 1.2% carbon), bearings (about 1% carbon, with chromium) and rails (about 0.7% carbon, cut a length for an anvil) are good steel; reinforcing bar is mild steel, wire rope is high-carbon steel wire; copper comes from electric wire and cable, motor and transformer windings and water pipes; brass from taps, valves, pipe fittings and cartridge cases; aluminium from window and door frames, cookware and drink cans; lead from wheel balance weights, old water pipes and cable sheaths. Dangers: never heat or cut gas cylinders, fire extinguishers, aerosol cans, lighters, shock absorbers, gas springs, sealed pipes and hollow parts or fuel tanks; galvanised parts give off zinc fumes when heated, causing metal fume fever, so grind the coating off or soak in vinegar for a day or two first; lead and cadmium are poisonous and old brake pads may contain asbestos; burning magnesium alloy gets fiercer with water and cannot be put out with water; damp scrap put into molten metal causes a steam explosion; capacitors, batteries and lithium batteries may discharge, leak acid or catch fire; do not burn the insulation off copper wire; work outdoors in a ventilated place, standing upwind
svg.title: Identifying scrap metal

g.text: Identifying scrap metal: identify first, then dismantle, then melt
cut off a small piece, heat it to
cherry red, quench in water and
file it: file won't bite → high
④ Spark testing (grinding wheel or coarse file): stream length, colour, forks
a few small forks at the ends
→ The more the sparks burst, the higher the carbon and the better for knives and tools
→ Compare against a piece of known steel (such as a file or reinforcing bar) for a more accurate judgement
⑤ The metals in a scrapped car
Good steel (store separately): files (about 1.2% carbon), bearings (about 1% carbon,
with chromium), rails (about 0.7%, for an anvil)
Ordinary steel: reinforcing bar (mild steel, inconsistent composition, for things that
need no hardening), wire rope (high-carbon steel wire)
Copper: electric wire and cable, motor and transformer windings, water pipes;
keep anything that can stay as wire unmelted
Brass: taps, valves, pipe fittings, cartridge cases
Aluminium: window and door frames, cookware, drink cans (very thin, big melting losses;
Lead: wheel balance weights, old water pipes, cable sheaths
Never heat or cut sealed parts: gas cylinders, fire extinguishers, aerosol cans, lighters,
shock absorbers, gas springs, sealed pipes and hollow parts (they may hold water or gas), fuel tanks
Galvanised parts (iron sheet, pipes, screws with a white coating) give off zinc fumes when heated
→ metal fume fever (fever, chills, aching all over); before forging or welding, grind the coating off,
or soak in vinegar for a day or two (in a ventilated place)
Lead, cadmium (golden-yellow plating) and their fumes are poisonous; old brake pads may contain
asbestos; do not burn the insulation off copper wire
Magnesium alloy chips and melt burn fiercely, even more so with water: water cannot put them out
Damp scrap put into molten metal → steam explosion; capacitors and batteries may discharge,
leak acid or catch fire when dismantled
Work outdoors in a ventilated place, stand upwind and wear protective gear
